passage:
Coach's note, college pool. Devika Nair, 3 October
Wasim trained with the 6 am group every weekday until his exams in August. Since then he hasn't been back. His locker still has his goggles and towel in it; I checked because the cleaners asked.
Today I passed him near the canteen. He saw me, went red and suddenly became very interested in his phone. When I said hello, he said, "Sorry, ma'am, I've been meaning to come. Next week, pakka." He said the same thing two weeks ago.
His friend Aman tells me Wasim changes the subject whenever swimming comes up and has stopped sitting at the café near the pool.
I don't think he's lazy. He looks embarrassed, as if coming back means facing how much ground he's lost.
What I did next: I sent him a short message. "No catching up needed. Just come on Friday and float for fifteen minutes. Your goggles are waiting."

qa.q: What is still in Wasim's locker?
qa.a: His goggles and towel.

qa.q: Why might Wasim go red and look at his phone when he sees the coach?
qa.a: He seems ashamed of not coming back, and seeing the coach reminds him of a goal he feels he has failed.

qa.q: Why does Devika's message fit this stage?
qa.a: It removes the pressure to catch up and asks only for fifteen minutes of floating, so restarting doesn't feel like facing a failure.

qa.q: What might Aman notice about Wasim?
qa.a: Aman sees Wasim dodge any talk of swimming and avoid the café near the pool, and may be puzzled or worried by the change.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding a lapsed swimming routine and the coach, with shame making the return feel like confronting failure.

passage:
Sunday
The Spanish notebook is still on my desk under a pile of laundry, which is exactly where I put it so I wouldn't have to see it.
Twenty-three days since my last lesson. The app sent a reminder this morning and I swiped it away so fast.
At lunch Zubin asked, "How's the Spanish going? Say something!" I laughed, said "Hola", and asked about his internship before he could ask anything else. My face was burning.
I told everyone in July I'd be conversational by Diwali. Now opening that notebook feels like opening a report card I already know is bad. Every day I don't start, it gets heavier.
Maybe tomorrow. I wrote that yesterday too.
Ritu

qa.q: Where is Ritu's Spanish notebook?
qa.a: On the desk under a pile of laundry.

qa.q: Why did Ritu's face burn when Zubin asked about the Spanish?
qa.a: Ritu felt ashamed of having stopped after telling everyone about being conversational by Diwali, so the question felt like being found out.

qa.q: What small step could break the avoidance?
qa.a: Ritu could uncover the notebook and do one short lesson without trying to catch up, or tell Zubin honestly about the break and ask for company.

qa.q: What might Zubin have noticed at lunch?
qa.a: Zubin was probably just curious and friendly, and may have noticed the quick 'Hola' and change of subject without knowing the shame behind it.

grounding: Illustrates a neglected learning habit, a hidden notebook and dodged questions, where shame makes restarting feel like facing a bad report card.

passage:
Week one: Rehana's Spanish notebook sat on her desk, untouched since the flu. She walked past it every morning.
Week two: The notebook had slid under a pile of lecture notes. When Jahnavi asked at lunch, "How's the Spanish going? You were so into it," Rehana said, "Oh, busy with exams," and changed the subject fast.
Week three: Rehana saw the corner of the notebook poking out and felt her face go hot. Opening it would mean seeing the last date, forty days ago, and admitting she'd quit. So she didn't. She pushed the notes back over it and went to bed, heavy and restless.

qa.q: What had slid under a pile of lecture notes?
qa.a: Rehana's Spanish notebook.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling in week three when she saw the notebook?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and heavy, her face hot, dreading the reminder that she had quit.

qa.q: What small step could break the avoidance at this stage?
qa.a: Opening the notebook for just five minutes without looking back at the gap, treating it as a fresh start.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi be thinking when Rehana changes the subject?
qa.a: Jahnavi may sense something is off and feel curious or concerned, but not want to push.

grounding: Shows a young woman avoiding her untouched notebook and dodging questions about the goal, as shame makes restarting feel like facing failure.

passage:
Irfan, beta, you've stopped going to the gym and now you don't even talk about it? I know that silence. Let me tell you about my running shoes, when I was twenty.
I ran every morning for three months. Then I sprained my ankle. Two weeks off. When it healed, I looked at those shoes by the door and felt such shame. Like they were accusing me.
So I moved them. Into the cupboard. When my friends asked, "Still running, Rafiq?" I said, "Oh, off and on," and laughed it away.
Months passed like that. The longer I waited, the bigger the failure felt.
What got me out? My sister put the shoes by my bed and said, "Ten minutes. Just walk."

qa.q: Where did Rafiq move the running shoes?
qa.a: Into the cupboard.

qa.q: What was young Rafiq feeling on looking at the shoes by the door?
qa.a: Young Rafiq felt ashamed, as if the shoes were an accusation of failure.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point ended the avoidance?
qa.a: Rafiq's sister putting the shoes by the bed and suggesting just ten minutes of walking, which made restarting feel small.

qa.q: What might Rafiq's sister have been thinking when she moved the shoes?
qa.a: She was probably caring and a little impatient, wanting to make restarting easy for Rafiq.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling hiding running shoes and laughing off friends' questions, as shame made restarting feel like failure.

passage:
The hostel room was tiny, and Irfan's gym bag sat right in the middle of the floor, where he tripped on it every day. Two months untouched.
Ujjwal, his roommate, kicked it aside. "Aren't you going any more?"
"Exams," Irfan said, eyes on his phone.
"Exams finished three weeks ago."
"Then I'm tired."
When their friends talked about the gym at dinner, Irfan went quiet and ate faster. He knew what the trainer would say if he walked back in. He knew what the mirror would show.
That night he pushed the bag under the bed. It didn't make him feel better. It just made the room look bigger and his chest feel tighter.

qa.q: How long had Irfan's gym bag been untouched?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he pushed the bag under the bed?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and tight-chested, hiding the reminder instead of facing going back.

qa.q: What turning point could help Irfan at this stage?
qa.a: A very small restart, like one short visit, perhaps with Ujjwal, so going back doesn't feel like facing a big failure.

qa.q: What is Ujjwal noticing when he kicks the bag aside?
qa.a: Ujjwal notices Irfan's excuses keep changing, and may feel puzzled or concerned.

grounding: Shows a young man avoiding his untouched gym bag and going quiet when friends mention the gym, shame stretching the avoidance.

passage: The blue gym bag had been sitting by the door of Vaibhav's PG room in Koramangala for nineteen days. He stepped over it every morning. The running shoes inside still had mud on them from the last Sunday he had gone to the lake with the club. In the office canteen, when Tanuja asked, "Still training for the December run?", he said, "Work's been crazy," and started talking about a new web series. That night he muted the running club group without reading the messages. It wasn't that he didn't want to run. Going back meant facing the coach, the others, and the question of where he had been. Every day he stayed away made that question heavier, so he stayed away another day.

qa.q: How long had the gym bag been sitting by the door?
qa.a: Nineteen days.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav mute the running club group?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of his absence, and reading the messages would mean facing the question of where he had been.

qa.q: What small step could break the avoidance?
qa.a: He could tell Tanuja the truth or send one message to the club, making the return a short run rather than a big confession.

qa.q: How might Tanuja read Vaibhav's change of subject?
qa.a: Tanuja may simply think he is busy, not realising the goal has become something he is ashamed to talk about.

grounding: Shows an untouched gym bag and a goal avoided in conversation, with shame making the return feel like facing a failure.
